paragraphs: “I was going to Father’s, but I meant to stop at Katerina Ivanovna’s first.”

“To her, and to Father! Ha! What a coincidence! Why was I waiting for you? Why was I hungering and thirsting for you in every corner of my soul, even in my ribs? To send you to Father and to her, to Katerina Ivanovna, so that I’d be done with her and done with Father. To send an angel. I could have sent anyone, but I wanted to send an angel. And here you are, already on your way to see Father and her.”
“Did you really mean to send me?” cried Alyosha, looking distressed.
“Hold on! You knew it! And I can see you understand everything at once. But be quiet, be quiet for a bit. Don’t be sorry, and don’t cry.”
Dmitri stood up, thought for a moment, and put his finger to his forehead.
“So she asked you to come? Wrote you a letter or something, and that’s the only reason you’re going to her? You wouldn’t go otherwise?”
“Here’s her note.” Alyosha took it out of his pocket. Mitya skimmed through it.

“And you were going the back way! Oh, gods, I thank you for sending him by the back way, and he came to me like the golden fish to the silly old fisherman in the fable! Listen, Alyosha, listen, brother! Now I’m going to tell you everything, because I have to tell someone. I’ve told an angel in heaven already, but I want to tell an angel on earth. You are an angel on earth. You’ll hear me out, and judge me, and forgive me. That’s what I need, for someone above me to forgive. Listen! Say two people break away from everything on earth and fly off into the unknown, or at least one of them does. And before flying off, or going to ruin, he comes to somebody else and says, ‘Do this for me’—some favor never asked before, that could only be asked on one’s deathbed. Would the other refuse, if he were a friend or a brother?”
“I’ll do it. But tell me what it is, and be quick,” said Alyosha.

“Be quick! Hm!... Don’t rush, Alyosha, you’re always rushing and fretting. There’s no need to hurry now. The world has taken a new turn. Ah, Alyosha, what a shame you can’t understand ecstasy. But listen to me, saying that to him! As if you didn’t understand it. What an ass I am! What am I saying? ‘Be noble, O man!’—who says that?”
Alyosha made up his mind to wait. He felt that perhaps his task really was here. Mitya sank into thought for a moment, his elbow on the table and his head in his hand. Neither of them spoke.

“Alyosha,” said Mitya, “you’re the only one who won’t laugh. I’d like to start—my confession—with Schiller’s _Hymn to Joy_, _An die Freude_! I don’t know German, I only know that’s what it’s called. Don’t think I’m talking nonsense because I’m drunk. I’m not the least bit drunk. Brandy’s all very well, but it takes two bottles to get me drunk:
Silenus with his rosy face, Riding his stumbling ass.

But I haven’t drunk even a quarter of a bottle, and I’m not Silenus. I’m not Silenus, though I am strong,[1] because I’ve made a decision once and for all. Forgive the pun; today you’ll have to forgive me a lot worse than puns. Don’t worry. I’m not spinning this out. I’m making sense, and I’ll get to the point in a minute. I won’t keep you in suspense. Wait, how does it go?”
He lifted his head, thought for a minute, and began with feeling:

“Wild and fearful in his cavern Hid the naked cave-dweller, And the homeless nomad wandered, Laying waste the fertile plain. With spear and arrow threatening, The hunter roamed the woods.... Woe to all poor wretches stranded On those cruel and hostile shores!

“Down from lofty Mount Olympus Mother Ceres made her way, Searching through those savage countries For her lost child Proserpine. But the Goddess found no shelter, Met with no kind welcome there, And no temple stood to witness That the gods were worshipped here.

“From the fields and from the vineyards No fruits came to deck the feasts, Only the flesh of bloodstained victims Smoldered on the altar-fires, And wherever the grieving goddess Turned her melancholy gaze, Sunk in the vilest degradation Man displayed his loathsomeness.”
Mitya burst into sobs and grabbed Alyosha’s hand.

“My dear, my dear, in degradation, in degradation now, too. Man has a terrible amount to suffer on earth, a terrible amount of trouble. Don’t imagine I’m only a brute in an officer’s uniform, wallowing in dirt and drink. Hardly a thought goes through my head except of that degraded man—if only I’m not lying. May God grant I’m not lying and showing off. I think about that man because I am that man myself.
If he would cleanse his soul of vileness And reach for light and worth, He must turn and cling forever To his ancient Mother Earth.

But the trouble is, how am I to cling forever to Mother Earth? I don’t kiss her. I don’t lie on her breast. Should I become a peasant or a shepherd? I go on and on, and I don’t know whether I’m heading for shame or for light and joy. That’s the trouble, because everything in the world is a riddle! And whenever I’ve happened to sink into the lowest degradation (and it happens all the time), I always read that poem about Ceres and man. Has it reformed me? Never! Because I’m a Karamazov. When I leap into the pit, I go in headfirst with my heels in the air, and I’m glad to be falling in that shameful position, and proud of it. And in the very depths of the degradation I start a hymn of praise. Let me be cursed. Let me be vile and base, only let me kiss the hem of the veil that wraps my God. Even if I’m following the devil, I am Your son, O Lord, and I love You, and I feel the joy without which the world cannot stand.

Joy everlasting feeds the soul Of all that was created; Her secret ferment sets aflame The cup of life. At her command the grass Turned every blade to the light, And solar systems rose from chaos And from the dark of night, Filling the realms of boundless space Beyond the sage’s sight. At bountiful Nature’s kindly breast All things that breathe drink Joy, And birds and beasts and creeping things All follow where she leads. Her gifts to man are friends in need, The wreath, the foaming must; To angels, a vision of God’s throne; To insects, sensual lust.

But enough poetry! I’m in tears, so let me cry. It may be a piece of foolishness that anyone else would laugh at. But you won’t laugh. Your eyes are shining, too. Enough poetry. Now I want to talk to you about those insects, the ones God gave “sensual lust.”
To insects, sensual lust.

I am that insect, brother, and it was said about me in particular. All of us Karamazovs are such insects, and, angel though you are, that insect lives in you, too, and will stir up a storm in your blood. Storms, because sensual lust is a storm—worse than a storm! Beauty is a terrible, awful thing! It is terrible because it can’t be fathomed and never can be, since God gives us nothing but riddles. Here the boundaries meet and all contradictions lie side by side. I’m not an educated man, brother, but I’ve thought a lot about this. The mysteries there are—it’s terrible! Too many riddles weigh men down on earth. We have to solve them as best we can, and try to come out of the water dry. Beauty! I can’t bear the thought that a man of lofty mind and heart starts with the ideal of the Madonna and ends with the ideal of Sodom. What’s still more awful is that a man with the ideal of Sodom in his soul doesn’t give up the ideal of the Madonna, and his heart may burn with that ideal, truly burn, just as it did in his innocent youth. Yes, man is broad, too broad, in fact. I’d make him narrower. The devil only knows what to make of it! What the mind finds shameful, the heart finds beautiful, and nothing else. Is there beauty in Sodom? Believe me, for the vast mass of mankind, beauty is found in Sodom. Did you know that secret? The awful thing is that beauty is mysterious as well as terrible. God and the devil are fighting there, and the battlefield is the human heart. But a man always talks about his own ache. Listen, now, let’s get to the facts.”
